content:
Let the two equilateral triangles be \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), and suppose their union could form a square \(S\).

1. Consider a corner \(P\) of \(S\), whose angle is \(90^\circ\).
2. If \(P\) lies inside an edge of either triangle, part of that triangle would extend outside the \(90^\circ\) corner of the square. Thus any triangle containing \(P\) must have \(P\) as a vertex.
3. One triangle at \(P\) covers only its \(60^\circ\) vertex angle, which is insufficient to fill the square’s \(90^\circ\) corner. Therefore both triangles must contain \(P\), so \(P\) must be a vertex of both triangles.
4. This would have to hold at all four corners of the square. Hence each equilateral triangle would need four vertices, but each has only three.

Thus a square cannot be the combined outline. The other outlines can be obtained by suitably touching or overlapping two identical equilateral triangles.
